what_this_is: The COMMODITY SHARE OF THE DOMESTIC ELECTRICITY UNIT RATE, derived from Ofgem's own published cap level model as (benchmark-consumption allowance minus nil-consumption allowance) / benchmark kWh, per component. The nil column IS the standing charge, so this is Ofgem's construction and not an apportionment invented here.
why_it_was_needed: The shift-response bridge converts a tariff pass-through into the price ratio a household faces, and needs the commodity share of the UNIT RATE. The knowledge map carried wholesale ~40% of the BILL -- a different denominator. This closes that gap.

basis.vat: Components are EX-VAT, and VAT ON ELECTRICITY IS NOT A CONSTANT: it is 5% except from 2026-10-01 to 2027-03-31, where it is ZERO under the Government's announcement, as stated in the v1.31 model's own `1a` note and visible in the workbook (for October-December 2026 the model's GB-average INCLUDING-VAT electricity row equals its ex-VAT row, while gas on the same row still carries 5%). A caller converting the ex-VAT unit rates published here to an including-VAT figure at a flat 1.05 is wrong for those two periods. Shares are unaffected by VAT at any rate; unit rates are not.

benchmark_consumption.it_is_not_a_constant: THE DENOMINATOR CHANGED TWICE IN 2026 AND THE SHEET HEADER STATES ONLY THE LATEST OF THE THREE BASES. Every period here is divided by the benchmark consumption that applied to it, carried in `benchmark_kwh` on each period row so no reader has to infer it. Reading the header cell instead would divide 29 of the 33 periods by 2,500 rather than 3,100 and publish every historical unit rate 24% high -- while every SHARE stayed exactly right, because the divisor cancels out of a ratio. That is why this is stated beside the figures.

provenance.3100: The basis of the whole pre-2026 series, and CORROBORATED rather than asserted: the eight periods January 2024 - October 2025 that a published cap level exists for land within 0.5% at 3,100 kWh and 24% high at 2,500.
provenance.2700: Ofgem's benchmark-consumption decision of 21 November 2025, from P15b.
provenance.2500: Ofgem's 'review of typical domestic consumption values' decision of 27 May 2026, from P16b.
provenance.how_the_two_2026_values_are_held: Read from the model's own `1c Consumption adjusted levels` table, which states them as figures against named date ranges rather than in prose, and re-checked against that table on every run: a disagreement REFUSES to publish rather than warning, because a fourth basis arriving unnoticed would inflate a whole unit-rate series while every share stayed right.

basis.regional_treatment: median across distribution regions, with the full spread beside it

headline.scope: periods with the cap actually in force, i.e. from 2019-01-01
headline.reading: The commodity share of the electricity unit rate is ABOVE 0.40 in every period the cap has actually been in force, which is the direction the shift-response finding predicted from the denominators. It is not a scalar: it runs from roughly 0.41 in the calm periods before the gas crisis to roughly 0.81 at the January 2023 peak, so a caller citing one value must name the cap period it belongs to. THIS CLAIM IS KEYED TO A WINDOW -- see `covers` -- and the window grows with every Ofgem edition. It is re-derived from the periods actually read on every run, so a future period below 0.40 moves `min_share` here rather than leaving this sentence standing over evidence that no longer supports it.
headline.the_backcast_is_not_the_law: Ofgem's model also carries pre-2019 columns it labels 'for illustration only' -- a cap level for periods in which no cap existed. Several fall BELOW 0.40. They are published here for completeness and excluded from this headline, because reading them as cap periods would make the claim above false in the flattering direction.

which_periods_the_cross_check_reaches.what_that_means: A basis listed in `bases_with_no_cross_checked_period` has NO period whose derived unit rate could be compared with a published cap level, because ofgem_default_tariff_cap_windows.json does not reach it. Those periods' unit rates rest on the model's own consumption table alone. Their SHARES are unaffected: a share is a ratio and the divisor cancels, so it is right whatever the benchmark is.

source_check.publication: Ofgem Default Tariff Cap level model, Default-tariff-cap-level-v1.31.xlsx
source_check.how_to_recheck: THE URL ABOVE IS A VERSION HISTORY PAGE, NOT THE WORKBOOK, and it is NOT the page this artefact cited until 2026-09-07. That one (/energy-policy-and-regulation/policy-and-regulatory-programmes/default-tariff-cap) returns 200 and carries exactly one .xlsx link -- the Annex 9 levelisation workbook -- so the old recipe, 'find the cap level model link there', could never terminate in anything but cannot_tell. A 200 serving nothing on the subject reads exactly like a working check. GET the URL above and take the HIGHEST v<major>.<minor> across every link matching Default[-_]tariff[-_]cap[-_]level OR Energy-price-cap-levels-pre-levelised-rates-model: the series is published under BOTH names (v1.30 under the second), so a check keyed to the filename stem rather than to the version number misses editions. If the highest is above `version_token`, the shares here were derived from a superseded model.

checked_for_supersession.note: Settled from `superseded` on 2026-09-07 by FETCHING v1.31 from the publisher (https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-08/Default-tariff-cap-level-v1.31.xlsx, HTTP 200, 5,319,726 bytes) and re-deriving every period from it. This artefact now carries all 33 columns the model publishes, to October-December 2026; it carried 21, to October-December 2023. NONE OF THE 21 MOVED, at any decimal place published, in any of the three payment methods -- so the extension added coverage and corrected nothing, which is what the finding that opened this predicted and registered in advance. THE DIVISOR RULE IS NOT THE TWO-BASIS ONE THAT FINDING STATED. There are THREE bases, not two: 3,100 kWh to December 2025, 2,700 from January 2026 (P15b, Ofgem's decision of 21 November 2025), and 2,500 only from July 2026 (P16b, the 'review of typical domestic consumption values' decision of 27 May 2026). The sheet's header cell states 2,500 alone, and the note beside it -- which the finding read -- predates the second revision and is itself incomplete. Applying that finding's rule verbatim would have divided January-June 2026 by 2,500 instead of 2,700 and published those two periods 8% high, silently, because a share is a ratio in which the divisor cancels. The schedule is now re-checked against the model's own `1c` consumption table on every run and REFUSES to publish on disagreement.
